This paper addresses the matters of suicide and euthanasia. What one believes about living and dying will have a determining influence on whether we/they will embrace or oppose death for themselves or others. A powerful mixture of transference and countertransference feelings is brought into play when the specter of death rises to haunt the therapeutic situation. All of us, analysts included, may be confounded by the complex of moral and philosophical issues and by the feelings they tend to evoke. Our attitude toward our own or another's decision to die is inextricably bound to the question as to who should make the decision regarding our own life or those of others. The crux of the countertransference resistance, the source of the difficulty we have in allowing others to die by their own choice, lies in the fact that we do not want them to die because of the effect their death will have on us.

There are some people who like to sit in the audience and enjoy the theater. Other people like to view the production from backstage. Douglas Kirsner, an Australian academic, provides an intimate unpolished portrait of life in four psychoanalytic institutes.

As Kirsner unfolds his sometimes unsavory tale of backstage psychoanalytic life, the reader searches for the author's bias, in what from a quick reading might appear to be another attempt at “psychoanalytic bashing.” However, when one considers Kirsner's reliance on documents, his 100 interviews over a ten-year period, and his otherwise scholarly approach, the reader may reach his/her own opinion and/or evaluation of Kirsner's conclusions.

Kirsner studied the New York Psychoanalytic Institute, the “Boston split” (the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and the Psychoanalytic Institute of New England East), the Chicago Psychoanalytic, and the Los Angeles Psychoanalytic Society and Institute.

The history of the New York Psychoanalytic Institute is especially important for modern psychoanalytic students because it provides a view of the context in which Hyman Spotnitz trained. The multiple conflicts and power struggles between the American analysts and the European emigres are well delineated. A parallel power struggle over the selection of training analysts is especially fascinating.

“What difference does psychoanalysis make to our understanding of ethical life?” This question is the focus of Lear's new book, the text of the three Tanner Lectures on Human Values which he recently delivered at Cambridge University—a place where, Lear notes in his

101

concluding acknowledgments, he discovered as a young man that philosophy is “an activity of the soul,” rather than merely the study of other people's thought. This commitment to philosophy as a way of life and a determinant of character rather than an abstract intellectual exercise pervades this book and informs the dialogue with psychoanalysis which Lear continues to advance so eloquently. With richness and depth, and a deceptively simple elegance, Lear addresses issues that arise in the consideration of Classical ethical theories, as he attempts to enhance our philosophical understanding of human nature (the basis for any theory about how human beings should live) with Freudian insights about the unconscious. In the process, he raises intriguing questions and suggests novel ways of thinking about some of the most fundamental concepts of both philosophy and psychoanalysis.

In his first chapter, Lear concentrates on “Happiness”—the goal and the identifying characteristic of the ethical life, according to Aristotle. As a philosopher/psychoanalyst, he is particularly taken with the Aristotelian emphasis on ethics as character-formation. As Lear explains, “The attraction of this character-based approach is that it purports to account for ethical life in terms of the lived realities of human motivation and judgment” (p. 2). Yet, he contends, although it may seem reasonable at first to assume that it might be possible to retain an ethics which is “Aristotelian in spirit” even as we incorporate the unconscious into our view of human nature, such an approach fails in the final analysis because “the unconscious is too disruptive to be contained in any straightforward account of character formation” (p. 3).

Lear argues that psychoanalysis is not just “one more science among others.” In fact, he agrees with those critics who maintain that “psychoanalysis is not another science in any normal sense.” To view it as such, says Lear, would lead to a type of complacency and detachment which would run counter to the necessarily disturbing “transformation of the soul” which takes place in the process of psychoanalysis—when we uncover disturbing things about ourselves while grappling with resistance and repression. We cannot, according to Lear, “keep the unconscious at a distance,” even as we theorize about it. And, when we consider Aristotle's psychologically based (rather than rule-based) ethics from our post-Freudian vantage point, “[t]he question … becomes, not ‘What do we have to add to Aristotle?’ but rather ‘What is already there in Aristotle's ethics, disturbing the self-presentation, yet not quite conscious of itself?’” (p. 5).

Arnold Bernstein has had a love affair of over half a century with psychoanalysis and with its founder, Sigmund Freud. His knowledge of Freud and his writings is prodigious but is experienced as intimate. Bernstein is also in love with words and with the precision of lucidly expressed ideas. He has a supple, far ranging, inquiring mind as evidenced in the breadth of issues addressed and examined in these papers and in the crystalline clarity of their exposition.

His dedication to and belief in the practice of psychoanalysis as a healing modality is legendary and is eloquently attested to in the paper “Beyond Countertransference: The Love That Cures.” Bernstein describes this love as the analyst's steadfast adherence to the principles of sound practice and by the requirements of the treatment rather than by his own feelings. Bernstein notes that in any other context, a renunciation of this degree is generally recognized as a loving act. Bernstein strongly suggests that it is not the therapist's feelings that cure but what happens between the two protagonists in the analytic encounter. “It is the process itself that cures!”

In two closely related papers, “The Analyst's Fear of Acting Out” and “The Fear of Compassion,” Bernstein deplores the fact that literal misreadings of Freud's statements on the countertransference and “the rule of abstinence” have deprived analysts of the privilege of having compassion for the helplessness and suffering of their patients and of the option of behaving compassionately toward them. He offers two brief case examples. With the first, early in his career, his fear of enacting a countertransference resistance prevented him from responding with kindness to a patient overwhelmed in a serious breakdown.

There are unmistakable evidences of personal confession in Freud's interpretation of the Oedipus story. Freud identifies himself with Oedipus and concludes that everybody does. Without challenging the validity of the Oedipus complex, what strikes us is that his observations about Oedipus Rex appear to be fatally and unmistakably flawed. Neither the myth nor the play by Sophocles shows incest or parricide as “wishes” of Oedipus. A fair and objective reading of the myth reveals unequivocally that it is the fears of King Laius, his father, not the lust of the son, Oedipus, that sets into motion the tragic chain of events upon which the myth rests!

Freud derived his interpretation from the play by Sophocles rather than the myth proper. The play and the myth differ in an essential way. The myth begins before the birth of Oedipus whereas the play begins after the death of Laius, his father. The play begins, as it were, where the myth leaves off. Freud likens the action of the play to the work of a psychoanalysis. Since Freud identifies with Oedipus it was natural that he should reconstruct the story in terms of his own life history, rather than from the more objective point of view in the Greek myth itself.

Fear of acting out on their own part and on the part of their patients are among the problems that most beset analysts who are insecure or inexperienced. Some therapists enforce the proscription against “acting out” either within or between sessions too literally as a result of their own anxieties and countertransference resistances—thus acting-out themselves. It is important for therapists to recognize the difference between rational actions required by the vicissitudes of life and those that are inimical to the client and analyst. The analytic task can sometimes only be accomplished by analyzing acting-out rather than by prohibiting it. Excessive zeal in enforcing the rule against acting out often is an acting out on the part of the analyst of panic, guilt, neurotic anxiety, self interest or an unconscious need to control the client's conduct.

Of all the dilemmas patients create for their parents and their analysts, those involving sex and anger are the most problematic. From its inception psychoanalysis has been rooted in the problems generated by mismanagement of these instincts, both by the patient and in the analyst. A parallel may be drawn between certain feelings generated in a mother's response to an infant's needs and the countertransference feelings aroused in a psychoanalyst in response to a patient's needs. Analysts, like parents, are faced with two mutually dependent tasks: how to deal with their patients' feelings and how to deal with their own. When parents cannot respond adequately to their own hostile and sexual drives, they cannot supply their children with a model of how to cope with such impulses. In order to provide patients with the psychic equivalent of adequate mothering during analysis, so that they are able to grow to maturity, analysts must have grown to maturity themselves. Analysts must be reasonably free of neurotic anxiety; that is to say, have reached the phase of psychosexual development that Karl Abraham and Wilhelm Reich referred to as the genital phase. For the genital analyst, treatment is a reciprocal relationship from which the analyst derives pleasure and satisfaction, while at the same time endeavoring to relieve the patient's suffering.

Long-term treatment adds a dimension to the treatment process that makes it possible to accomplish long-term goals that brief psychotherapy does not even address. The author identifies and describes a new phenomenon connected to this, an emergence of the “wonder child.” These children are an unanticipated and unreported by-product of long-term psychotherapeutic treatment. They result from the beneficial impact of psychoanalytic treatment upon children whose parents are being analyzed. In some cases the most visible results of a patient's treatment are to be seen in the next generation. The appearance of such a “wonder child” is evidence that the intergenerational repetitions have been interrupted and the transmission of pathology from generation to generation has been halted. Patients are “shaped” by their analysts and in turn shape their children, much as analysts are shaped by their own analysts and supervisors. Thus a kind of retroflective-transference occurs, a transference from the analysis to the world, which is the reverse of the usual transference. As a result of this retroflective-transference, patients begin to act in a more accepting, objective, nonjudgmental, warm and loving way toward others. In doing so, they become better parents to their children, better children to their parents, and better friends to everyone they know.

This paper takes as its point of departure Freud's comment that after all, psychoanalysis is actually a cure effected through love. It tries to show how the process we call psychotherapy is a particular form of love that is designed to cure; and furthermore that it is not the therapist's love that cures but the process of psychotherapy itself. The specific property that marks mental health is the capacity to act in a loving way. Pathological narcissism interferes with this capacity. In order to effect a cure an analyst must be capable of having the “right” feelings and must provide patients with a context in which they may feel safe enough to say everything. In doing so analysts may be called upon to overcome or to transcend their own transferences and countertransferences.

In this case presentation the focus is on the examination of the countertransference and counterresistance problems faced by an analyst in an effort to generate progress in the treatment of a paranoid patient. Procedures that were employed depart considerably from the paradigm of classical psychoanalysis, because traditional means had proved fruitless and the nature of the patient's paranoia was such that it had taken the form of a full-blown delusional system with me as its central character. My induced feelings shaped my treatment strategy in working with this patient. The use of interpretations was avoided in favor of focusing almost exclusively on reacting to transference communications and resistances and joining his resistances. This succeeded in dissolving his major resistance to communication so he could begin to talk.

Since 1940 a cultural revolution has taken place regarding sexuality. Even the most superficial examination of the behavior of elementary school children and teenagers reveals this. One result has been that today's children do not pass through childhood with quite the same attitudes toward sex as their parents did, i.e., a sexual latency period. At the same time the classical psychoneurotic that Freud described is being displaced by patients with borderline and impulse disorders. The question is raised as to whether the decrease in neurotic patients and the increase in the number of impulse disorders may be attributed to the gradual disappearance of the classical latency period.
